examples.title: Supplied model: Plot C pH 6.8, loam
examples.situation: The source's teaching model reports pH 6.8 and loam, then names tomatoes and corn.
reasoning: Keep pH and texture labelled supplied model rather than personal measurements.
Explain what near-neutral pH and loam texture tend to suggest, and list the unmeasured site/crop constraints.
Treat annual compost and pH monitoring every 1–2 years as examples to check, not compulsory prescriptions.
examples.takeaway: A model supports report writing; it cannot certify all soil conditions.

examples.title: Separate pH 5.8 sandy-loam case
examples.situation: A different case uses pH 5.8, sandy loam, gritty feel and an approximately 0.5-inch ribbon.
reasoning: State the acidity classification source instead of relying on a vague adjective.
Discuss potatoes and strawberries as candidates; corn is conditional on crop/site requirements.

The source's illustrative pH 5.8→6.5 lime-target rationale names corn and alfalfa. Check the actual crop target, an appropriate lime-requirement test and material/site information before turning that example, agricultural limestone or a compost plan into a field recommendation; no dose is established by pH alone.
examples.takeaway: Different source examples and the learner's real Plot C belong in separate report records.

examples.title: A retry can still need more practice
examples.situation: The sample was prepared well, but the pH meter was calibrated incorrectly and its reading is unreliable.
reasoning: The trainer credits observed preparation only under its own criterion and identifies calibration as the unmet one.
The learner studies the actual meter procedure and demonstrates a fresh calibration and measurement.
The trainer records what was actually seen, including another 'not yet demonstrated' if a required check still fails.
examples.takeaway: A new attempt creates new evidence, not automatic success.
